stem: In the 10% of cases where Perthes disease is bilateral, what is the usual pattern of onset?

options.text: Onset only after the first hip has fully healed
Onset only in children under 3 years of age
Persistent onset without a symptom-free interval

explanation: Sequential onset at different times is the usual pattern in bilateral Perthes disease, with one hip affected first and the other involved later.
rationale: Bilateral Perthes disease typically affects the hips at different times rather than presenting together.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect because bilateral Perthes disease usually does not start in both hips at exactly the same time.
optionExplanations.B: Correct because one hip is usually affected first and the second hip becomes involved later, often months apart.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because the second hip may become involved before the first hip has fully recovered.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because bilateral involvement can occur across the usual age range for Perthes disease.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because the key pattern is delayed involvement of the second hip, not continuous simultaneous onset.

source.hint: Recall how the timing of diagnosis usually differs between the two affected joints.
